issue: PMAT-240 (closes forjar#530) — the SIGPIPE class, over the tree rather than three files. A pipeline whose right-hand side can exit before its left finishes (grep -q, grep -m, head, jq -e) makes the left take SIGPIPE; under `set -o pipefail` it returns 141 and a gate reports UNMEASURED at random, which gate T did on about one run in three. PMAT-239 fixed three instances and wrote a rule over THREE FILES; its own census found eighteen more and thirteen were still there. Fifteen sites are closed here — the rule itself found three the census never listed — and the rule now walks every stage of every pipeline in every script under scripts/, libraries included.

quorum.rounds: one round of three sandboxed agy quorum lanes with --not-before pinned to the dispatch instant. All three returned, exits 0/0/0, durations 311s/433s/441s, verdicts 3/3 FAIL.
quorum.kill_rule: six claims and the standing instruction. THE RULE HAD FOUR HOLES, each openable with one line of shell, and all three lanes found at least two. A rule against a hazard class is only worth the holes it does not have, and these four survived a careful author, a census and a first round of testing — they did not survive three readers each handed one instruction. The instruction also caught a receipt describing a log that did not contain what it claimed, which is now three for three across this release.
refuted_claims: That a `#` in a line is a comment — `cat f | grep " # " | head -1` has its `#` inside a string, and cutting the line there took the `head` stage with it. The pipeline vanished from the rule entirely.
That a `|` in a line is a pipe — `echo " | head "` was reported as fatal. A rule that fires on text which runs nothing is a rule people learn to ignore.
That a pipeline is one line — `cat f \` plus `| head -1` on the next line is one pipeline written on two, and the rule saw two lines with no pipe between them.

That `||` is two pipes — found while fixing the above. `cmd || head -1` split into three stages with an empty one between, and the `head` read as a right-hand side when it is a FALLBACK: nothing pipes into it.

That the library case proves the library is walked — the planted pipeline went at the END of the file, where a rule reading only a file's last line would pass. It is in the middle now and the case asserts the reported LINE NUMBER.

That every rewrite preserves behaviour — the old sed anchors the closing quote at end of line, so `version = "1.29.0" # a comment` (valid TOML) yields NOTHING and the script fails. The awk reads 1.29.0. A behaviour CHANGE in the right direction, now recorded as a change in all three scripts and named as an unpinned gap.
That six gates passed 'either way' — they were run at HEAD only and the log holds one run. Third time in this release a receipt has been caught describing a file that did not contain what it claimed.
lane_errors: The delegate stopped at its 30-turn limit while reducing, after all three lanes completed. Ninth occurrence in this session at the same point.

crux.verdict: accept(the question is whether a hazard is fixed at its instances or at its class, and every surveyed system answers the class. Nix makes a whole category of build non-determinism impossible by construction rather than auditing for it [X]. Bazel's sandbox makes an undeclared input a build error everywhere rather than a lint on the files someone remembered [X]. systemd's unit ordering is a graph the manager refuses cycles in, not a convention [X]. Debian's Lintian runs over every package rather than the ones a maintainer touched [X]. PMAT-239 fixed three instances and scoped its rule to three files, which is the shape all four reject, and eighteen sites survived it. Where forjar remains WORSE than all four: this rule is TEXTUAL — it reads shell as strings, and a pipeline built by `eval` or whose command arrives in a variable is invisible. None of the four relies on reading its own source as text; they change the substrate so the hazard cannot be expressed. A shell gate cannot do that, which is an argument about the substrate rather than about this rule.)

tool_defects_found: `cargo test` in a `--shared` clone reuses the shared target directory's binaries, so a proof run there can measure a stale rule. Setting CARGO_TARGET_DIR to a fresh path is the fix, and the first two attempts at this ticket's red proof were both wrong because of it.
